LegacyMigrator · branch claude/dashboard · 4 Nov 2026

The control-room dashboard

A read-only website that shows judges what the pipeline proved: every legacy job, every AI attempt, and the exact rows where the new code disagreed with the old system. It reads one JSON file. It never runs anything, so it works offline on the finale laptop and can be hosted anywhere.

87 KBgzipped app code, fonts bundled, no CDN at runtime
17 / 17statements sqlglot "converted" (real run)
7 / 17of those Spark's own parser rejects (real run)
0console errors or sideways scroll across 4 pages × 2 widths × 2 themes
Real vs sample. The dashboard ships two data files. real.json holds only what has happened: the Sale translation matched Integration.Sale_Staging on 5,224 rows × 26 columns, nothing else compared yet. sample.json is an invented demo story (attempt timelines, mismatches, holdout results) and the app shows a striped "Sample data" banner whenever it's loaded. No real City, Movement or holdout results existed when I finished.

What I built, newest ideas first

1. The dashboard doesn't trust the status field either

The pitch is "the AI never grades its own work". It would be odd if the dashboard then believed whatever "status": "verified" a file says. So it works out every verdict from the per-table results diff.reconcile() produced. A job only shows as Verified if its latest attempt passed every table on dev and holdout data. If a file claims verified without that evidence, the job shows Unconfirmed with a warning. I tested this by editing Movement's status to "verified" in a copy of the sample: the headline stayed at "2 of 3" and the job page showed the warning. scripts/check_results.py applies the same rule from the command line.

2. The attempt timeline, with the AI's feedback shown word for word

Each job page tells the story the demo needs: attempt 1 crashed (Spark has no UPDATE), attempt 2 got City Key wrong on 1,190 rows, attempt 3 matched on dev and holdout. Between attempts it says whether an error or a diff summary was sent back. Under each failed attempt is the exact text the AI was given, so anyone can check that holdout data never appears in it.

3. Mismatches in plain words, then the raw rows

Differences read like "Sale Staging Key 1027 · City Key · old system said 18942 · new code said 0". Below that are the whole rows reconcile() found with no identical twin. For readability, each old row is lined up with the most similar new row and the differing cells are highlighted. That pairing is labelled as display only. It never feeds a verdict.

4. "What changed since the last attempt"

The Code tab shows the T-SQL and PySpark side by side with syntax highlighting. One toggle switches the PySpark side to a line diff against the previous attempt. In the demo story that shows the AI's planted "optimisation" being removed: three red lines, one green line.

5. A real transpiler probe instead of a paraphrase

The devlog says sqlglot reported 141/141 statements converted, yet the output still had T-SQL-only syntax. I made that reproducible: scripts/sqlglot_probe.py transpiles every statement in our three procedures with strict errors on, then hands each result to Spark's own SQL parser. Result: 17 of 17 "converted", 7 of 17 still rejected by Spark (six UPDATE … FROM, one DELETE s FROM). The "How it works" page shows each rejected statement and Spark's real error. To be fair to sqlglot, the probe fills in T-SQL variables first, so they aren't what fails.

6. A contract, a checker, and a converter for the sibling branch's output

docs/results-contract.md defines the file. It stores what reconcile() already returns, unchanged, plus attempts, code, errors, feedback, timings and ignored columns with reasons, so the owner's loop.py can build it with a plain json.dump(..., default=str). Late in the session, claude/test-bench added migrator/check.py with its own output format and stricter checks. I added an optional extra_checks field to the contract and wrote scripts/check_to_results.py. I tested it on output from check.py's real check_table(), which calls the real diff.reconcile().

Real outputs

sqlglot vs Spark's parser

$ python scripts/sqlglot_probe.py
{ "sqlglot_version": "30.29.0", "statements": 17,
  "sqlglot_succeeded": 17, "spark_parse_rejected": 7 }
MigrateStagedSaleData.sql DELETE: Spark says [PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR] Syntax error at or near 's': extra input 's'.
MigrateStagedSaleData.sql UPDATE: Spark says [PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR] Syntax error at or near 'FROM'.
... (2 per procedure for City and Movement, 3 for Sale)

Run with pyspark 4.3.0 in a scratch virtualenv. The ten statements Spark did accept still aren't proven to give the same answer. sqlglot quietly swapped SYSDATETIME() for CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), for example, and an UPDATE on a plain Parquet table won't run without Delta. A converter can't catch any of that. Running both jobs can.

The checker also caught a real mismatch on the first converter run. check.py compares ignored columns in a masked form ("filled in or empty") and lists them as compared, which my contract forbids. The converter now lists them as ignored and adds an extra check that says they were still checked for filled vs empty.

How to run it on the Mac

Needs Node.js 20 or newer. If node -v fails:

brew install node

Get the branch and start the dashboard:

git fetch origin
git checkout claude/dashboard
cd dashboard
npm ci
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:5173. Press ? for shortcuts. Switch data files with the dropdown in the header, or open http://localhost:5173/?data=real.

For the finale (offline):

npm run build
npm run preview

Then open http://localhost:4173. Or copy dashboard/dist/ anywhere and run python3 -m http.server -d dist 8000.

Rebuild the data files after changing a translation or the sample story (from the repo root, Python 3.10 is fine):

python scripts/build_dashboard_data.py
python scripts/check_results.py dashboard/public/data/*.json

Show real check.py results once claude/test-bench is merged and has run:

python migrator/check.py sale
python scripts/check_to_results.py sale
python scripts/check_results.py dashboard/public/data/results.json

Then add {"id": "results", "label": "Latest run", "path": "results.json"} to dashboard/public/data/manifest.json and set "default": "results".

Re-run the sqlglot probe (needs Java, which Spark needs anyway):

pip install sqlglot pyspark
python scripts/sqlglot_probe.py

Decisions and why

Static site, no backend
The app only reads results. A FastAPI server would add a process to start at the venue and code to maintain, and nothing to show for it. Static files open on any laptop with no internet and can be hosted anywhere. Fonts are bundled through @fontsource for the same reason.
Vite + React + TypeScript, five runtime dependencies, exact versions
React because the devlog planned it. TypeScript because the types file doubles as a checklist for loop.py, and it reads close to Java. No router library (hash links are 40 lines), no UI kit, no chart library. highlight.js loads only SQL and Python.
Store reconcile() output unchanged
The owner writes loop.py and is learning Python. If the file is just "what reconcile() returned, lists trimmed", there's nothing to translate and nothing to get wrong. It's also more honest: the file holds evidence and the UI draws the conclusions.
Columns are ignored per job, not per table
The Sale job never writes Dimension.City, so there every City column is compared, including City Key. Ignoring a column everywhere would quietly weaken checks where they cost nothing.
"Verified", never "safe to switch"
My first draft said "Safe to switch". That overclaims what the devlog's Responsible AI note says. The page now says "Verified", and "How it works" explains that a pass isn't a proof and a parallel run on production data still matters.
Two data files instead of one mixed file
Mixing real and invented numbers in one file and marking which is which invites mistakes on stage. One file is fully real, the other is fully a story with a banner. The dropdown makes it obvious which one is showing.
Sample attempt code lives in scripts/dashboard_samples/
Never in jobs_pyspark/ or legacy_jobs/. Attempt 3 of the Sale story is read straight from the real jobs_pyspark/sale.py. Attempt 2 is built from it by a script that inserts one planted line and fails loudly if sale.py changes.

What didn't work, limits, and what's left

  • No new real results. I can't run SQL Server here, so the only verified fact is still Sale_Staging. City, Movement, the other seven Sale tables and all holdout numbers in the demo are invented. claude/test-bench had no docs/reports/data/ when I checked. It had check.py, which the converter now handles.
  • An identity claim to confirm. The reason given for ignoring Sale Key is that SQL Server doesn't roll identity numbers back, so two legacy runs give different keys. That's standard SQL Server behaviour, but nobody has shown it on our data yet. Running run_legacy.py sale twice and diffing the two after/ folders would settle it.
  • check.py keeps counts, not rows. Its output has counts and five examples per table, so after conversion the "whole rows" panel is empty and only the plain-language examples show. If check.py also kept ~20 of only_a/only_b, the dashboard would show them.
  • The probe covers 3 procedures (17 statements). The 141/141 figure comes from the devlog's earlier run on all 13 procedures. The page labels which number is which.
  • Lineage is hand-derived from the Sale SQL and labelled that way. The planned lineage step should replace it.
  • Bugs I hit and fixed. An effect that returned window.scrollTo()'s result crashed React's cleanup. Failing tables didn't open when you switched attempts, because React kept their state. My first probe blamed sqlglot for T-SQL variables, which wasn't fair, so variables are filled in now.
  • No automated UI tests in the repo. I checked with Playwright scripts in my scratch space, not a committed suite. A small screenshot test would be a good next step.

Suggestions for the hand-written files (not changed)

  • translate.py: the prompt has a typo, "froasm the SQL". The AI will cope, but it's in every prompt.
  • loop.py: write the file in docs/results-contract.md straight from each attempt. Run holdout only after dev passes, and never put holdout output into feedback. The trimming snippet in the contract doc keeps the file small when Fact.Sale fails on 200,000 rows.
  • check.py's masking idea (ignored columns must still be filled in on the same rows) is a good, cheap tightening of the ignore list. It may be worth folding into how loop.py calls reconcile().

Explaining this to the judges

This part is for you, for the video and for talking at the stand. No Spark knowledge needed.

The problem. Big companies run hundreds of old database jobs every night. They fill the tables that reports read from. Companies want to move them to a newer system called Spark, but each one has to be rewritten by hand, and nobody wants to switch off a job that works unless they're sure the new one does exactly the same thing.

What we do. An AI rewrites the job. Then we run the old job and the new job on exactly the same starting data and compare what comes out, row by row. The old job's real output is the answer key. The AI writes the code but never marks its own homework.

What the dashboard shows. The first screen says how many jobs are verified, for example "2 of 3 jobs verified on data the AI never saw". Click a job and you see its story: attempt 1 crashed, attempt 2 got the city wrong on 1,190 sales, attempt 3 matched every row. It shows real examples like "old system said city 18942, new code said 0", so you can see the check isn't just a green tick.

"Data the AI never saw". It's like a student who practises with an answer sheet. Passing the practice test proves less than passing an exam with new questions. We keep a second set of data, the holdout, that the AI is never shown. A job only counts as verified if it passes that too. The Movement job in the demo shows why: it passed the practice data and failed the holdout. The holdout differences aren't sent back to the AI, so a person takes over.

"Why not use an existing converter?" We tried a popular one, sqlglot. It said all 17 statements converted fine. Spark refused to even read 7 of them. A tool that says "success" when it isn't is the risk here. Our answer is to run the new code and compare its output with the old job's.

Be careful to say. The demo story uses made-up numbers (the yellow "Sample data" banner says so). The real result so far is one table, 5,224 rows × 26 columns, matched exactly. And "verified" means "matched on every dataset we tried", not a mathematical guarantee. We recommend running old and new side by side for a while before switching.

A 20-second script for the video. "This is the control room. Three legacy jobs, two verified on data the AI never saw. Here's Sale: the AI's first try crashed, its second got the city wrong on 1,190 rows, and the system caught it, showing exactly which rows. Third try: every row matches the old system, including on a test set the AI never saw."
